design_detail: Inpatient human laboratory study at a university general clinical research centre. Ten paid volunteers who used cocaine and alcohol completed five sessions in a double-blind, balanced crossover: ethanol 1.0 g/kg with deuterium-labelled cocaine-d5 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg/kg; ethanol 1.0 g/kg with cocaine placebo; and double placebo. In every session 7.5 mg of deuterium-labelled cocaethylene-d3 was infused at the same time as the cocaine or its placebo, as a tracer for working out how much cocaethylene the body formed. Ethanol (or orange juice alone) was drunk in five portions over 30 minutes; the cocaine infusion ran at a constant rate over 15 minutes, starting 1 hour after the first drink. Sessions were at least a week apart and participants stayed on the unit for 36 hours after dosing. Separately, 6 of the 10 returned 1 to 3 months later for a sixth session with cocaine 1.2 mg/kg and ethanol placebo; the authors state this session was neither blinded nor randomized, and its results are analysed as a subset comparison (n = 6). Labelled cocaine, cocaethylene and benzoylecgonine were measured in plasma and urine by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; breath ethanol, heart rate, blood pressure, rate-pressure product and spoken or computer-entered ratings were recorded.
can_establish: In 10 people who used cocaine and alcohol and were not dependent on drugs other than nicotine, what share of an intravenous cocaine dose given 1 hour after a substantial oral ethanol dose appeared as cocaethylene, how cocaethylene, cocaine and benzoylecgonine concentrations in plasma and urine changed across a four-fold range of cocaine study doses, and how heart rate, blood pressure and ratings changed in those same conditions relative to ethanol alone and double placebo.
cannot_establish: Whether cocaethylene itself caused any of the effects measured (it was never given alone at an active dose, and its formation cannot be separated from the presence of ethanol); whether the combination is more harmful than cocaine alone (no toxicity outcome, and the cocaine-alone comparison rests on 6 people in an unblinded session months later); what happens when alcohol is drunk after cocaine, at other ethanol doses, or by other routes; and whether any of this extends to the amounts and patterns people use outside a laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper advertisements and referral from people who had taken part in earlier studies; all were paid (pp. 171, 172). To obtain the 10 who were entered and tested, 53 applicants were screened out, by their own preference or by the investigators, most often for not having enough experience with substantial intravenous cocaine doses (pp. 172–173).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Had used cocaine and ethanol; not dependent by DSM-IV criteria on drugs other than nicotine; physical or mental conditions that might raise risk excluded after history, physical examination, screening blood chemistry and electrocardiogram. Written informed consent; approval by the university's human-research committee and the state research advisory panel (p. 171).
sample.demographics: Eight men and two women; mean age 34 (SD 7) years; mean weight 71 (SD 7) kg; eight Caucasian and two African-American (p. 172).
sample.attrition: No dropouts are reported from the five blinded sessions. Only 6 of the 10 took part in the later cocaine-alone session; how those six were chosen is not stated (p. 171).
sample.selection_effects: A small, experienced group selected for tolerating substantial intravenous doses: 53 of 63 applicants were screened out, mainly for too little experience with intravenous cocaine, the preferred route for all 10. None had ever sought treatment for cocaine-related problems, so this is not a treatment sample. Reported alcohol use was light: on average 13 g of ethanol a week (range 2–23 g), while the study's single ethanol dose of 1.0 g/kg is about 71 g at the mean weight, roughly five times the average reported weekly intake (editors' calculation from pp. 172–173). The results therefore describe a drinking exposure unlike these participants' own reported pattern.

exposure.measurement: Drugs given in the laboratory. Cocaine-d5, cocaethylene-d3, cocaethylene-d5, benzoylecgonine and ecgonine esters measured in plasma and urine by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry with deuterium-labelled internal standards; limits of quantitation 5 ng/ml in plasma and 10 ng/ml in urine for the listed compounds. Breath ethanol by infrared spectrophotometry, reported as blood ethanol in g/dl (p. 172). Participants' own use was self-reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Cocaine-d5 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg/kg or placebo by constant-rate intravenous infusion over 15 minutes, beginning 1 hour after the first drink; 7.5 mg cocaethylene-d3 infused over the same period from a separate syringe into the same line; ethanol 1.0 g/kg (80-proof vodka as a 15.8% wt/vol solution in orange juice) or orange juice alone, in five portions every 6 minutes over 30 minutes (pp. 171–172). The authors state the 15-minute infusion was chosen so that it could be stopped if adverse effects appeared and was not intended to mimic how people use intravenous cocaine (p. 171). Self-reported own use: typical weekly cocaine about 905 mg (range 94–3500 mg); all had used at least 250 mg on one or more occasions; average 13 g of ethanol weekly (range 2–23 g) (pp. 172–173).
exposure.polysubstance: Extensive and quantified but not controlled: 7 of 10 smoked tobacco (mean 20 cigarettes daily); 8 smoked cannabis (mean 2.3 g per week, range 0.6–5.5 g); 3 used amphetamines (mean 375 mg weekly, range 62–1000 mg); 3 used heroin (56 mg weekly, range 50–62 mg); 1 used diazepam (5 mg weekly) (p. 173). None of these was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Asked to abstain from psychoactive drugs other than caffeine and nicotine for 24 hours before each session, and from cigarettes and caffeine from 2 hours before to 6 hours after dosing; admitted the day before each session and resident for 36 hours after (pp. 171–172). Verification is not described, and the authors report that on two occasions the amount of unlabelled cocaine metabolites in pre-dose urine exceeded the amount after the laboratory dose, which they take as evidence of use outside the study (p. 180).

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant served in all five blinded conditions, which included ethanol with cocaine placebo and a double placebo. The cocaine-alone condition (ethanol placebo with cocaine 1.2 mg/kg) was an open, non-randomized sixth session in 6 of the 10, 1 to 3 months later (p. 171).
comparison.matching: Within-person design; the deuterium labels allowed cocaine-derived cocaethylene-d5 to be told apart from the infused cocaethylene-d3 in the same session, so the drug and its metabolite did not have to be given on separate days (pp. 170–171).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic questions. For the rated effects, the pre-dose value in each session is the only baseline; tolerance from the participants' own use was not measured, and the authors raise lingering tolerance as a possible reason for small differences between conditions (p. 180).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group). Tobacco, cannabis and other drug use was recorded for all participants and not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma and urine concentrations and derived non-compartmental pharmacokinetic parameters (AUC to infinity by the trapezoidal then log-trapezoidal method, Cmax, Tmax, half-life, plasma and renal clearance, volume of distribution); fractional conversion of cocaine to cocaethylene from the ratio of cocaethylene-d5 to cocaethylene-d3 areas under the curve and the known 7.5 mg cocaethylene-d3 dose, corrected for molecular weights of 308 and 322. Heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure by automated monitor, and rate-pressure product as their product. Spoken 0–100 ratings of ethanol intoxication, cocaine intoxication and total intoxication; computer-entered 100 mm visual analogue ratings of drug combination liking and 'good' drug effect, anchored 0 (none) to 100 (most ever) (pp. 171–172).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assay limits of quantitation are given; assay precision is not reported in this paper. The rating scales are study-specific, have no norms, and the intoxication ratings were spoken aloud rather than entered privately.
outcomes.operationalization: Nothing is operationalized as harm or toxicity. 'Liking' and 'good drug effect' are single ratings; 'total intoxication' is a global rating covering all drugs given. Analyses are of change scores from the pre-dose value, as a time course and as each person's peak.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Each pharmacokinetic parameter in Tables 1–5 and each physiological and subjective measure was tested by repeated-measures ANOVA at P <= 0.05, with least-squares-means pairwise comparisons after a significant F test and the Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity only; urine molar amounts were compared with Wilcoxon matched-pairs tests (p. 172).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The five crossover sessions were double-blind, with ethanol-scented cotton in a double-walled container to mask the placebo drink. The sixth cocaine-alone session was neither blinded nor randomized (pp. 171, 180). Assays are objective; intoxication ratings were spoken to staff.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard deviations and P values; no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes; F statistics are not printed. Fractional conversion of cocaine to cocaethylene 17 ± 6% (mean ± SD), from a mean 1.8 mg of cocaethylene-d5 per 10 mg of cocaine-d5 (range 1.0–4.0 mg), with no significant difference between cocaine doses (p. 173). Cocaethylene-d5 Cmax 16.8 (SD 7.64), 30.1 (11.1) and 53.1 (15.0) ng/ml and AUC 57.4 (40.7), 109 (33.0) and 217 (62.7) h ng/ml at cocaine 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg, with dose-corrected values not differing (Table 3, p. 175). Cocaine-d5 Cmax 250 (73.0), 438 (151) and 891 (271) ng/ml (Table 1, p. 174). In the n = 6 comparison of cocaine 1.2 mg/kg with and without ethanol (Table 4, p. 176): cocaine half-life 1.91 (0.51) vs 1.29 (0.15) h (P < 0.02), renal clearance 2.53 (1.02) vs 1.53 (1.05) l/h (P < 0.02), amount excreted unchanged 2 630 000 vs 1 490 000 ng (P < 0.02), while AUC (1030 vs 1010) and Cmax (968 vs 823) did not differ; benzoylecgonine Cmax 452 (62.2) vs 652 (111) ng/ml (P < 0.01), urine concentration 7770 vs 14 800 ng/ml (P < 0.02) and amount excreted 18 500 000 vs 31 300 000 ng (P < 0.01).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person repeated-measures ANOVA on change scores.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: For the cocaine-alone comparison (n = 6) no physiological or subjective means, SDs or figure are shown: Fig. 4 plots only the five n = 10 conditions, and the text reports that comparison as P values alone (pp. 177–179). Diastolic blood pressure and rate-pressure product are described in words without data for that comparison.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 10 participants (6 for the cocaine-alone comparison), non-significant differences cannot be read as showing no difference; the authors attribute several null results to the small sample and large variability in ratings (p. 180).

interpretation_gap.results_show: When a 1.0 g/kg ethanol dose was drunk an hour before intravenous cocaine, about one-sixth of the cocaine dose (17 ± 6%) appeared as cocaethylene, in proportion to the cocaine dose across a four-fold range; cocaethylene peak concentrations (17–53 ng/ml) stayed far below the cocaine peaks (250–891 ng/ml) and peaked 1.3–1.6 hours after dosing. With ethanol present, less benzoylecgonine was formed and excreted and more cocaine was excreted unchanged. In the 6 people tested both ways, ratings of total intoxication and of drug liking were higher over the time course with ethanol than with cocaine alone, while peak ratings, blood pressure and rate-pressure product did not differ.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that participants liked and experienced more total intoxication after the combination than after either drug alone (p. 169). Against ethanol alone this rests on time-course analyses only: peak ratings of liking and good drug effect did not differ between ethanol alone and any cocaine condition (p. 179). Against cocaine alone it rests on 6 of the 10 people in an unblinded, non-randomized session held 1 to 3 months later, where cocaine intoxication across time and peak ratings did not differ (p. 179); the authors themselves note that expectation may have influenced those ratings (p. 180). The Discussion and Conclusions raise greater toxicity of cocaethylene than of benzoylecgonine as something that might increase risk, explicitly conditional on rat findings applying to humans (p. 179), and say the biotransformation may contribute to changes that might alter clinical presentation (p. 180); no toxicity, morbidity or clinical outcome was measured. The suggestion that lower benzoylecgonine could reduce the sensitivity of some urine screens near their cut-off is stated as a possibility requiring further study (pp. 179–180).

timeline.event: Jatlow et al. report cocaethylene in post-mortem and emergency-room blood after combined cocaine and ethanol use and show it is active at the dopamine transporter in rats and self-administered by monkeys
McCance et al. (as cited here, p. 170): intranasal cocaine with ethanol raised cocaine concentrations and produced greater rated effects than cocaine alone

Perez-Reyes (as cited here, p. 170) found no differences between cocaine alone and cocaine plus ethanol when ethanol was given after cocaine, which the authors contrast with their own order of administration
Multiple-dose study of concurrent cocaine and alcohol, used here as the comparison for intranasal dosing
Intravenous cocaethylene compared directly with cocaine in people with cocaine dependence: less potent than cocaine on heart rate and on rated effects
Review of the effects of concurrent alcohol and cocaine use

replication.where_it_stands: By the authors' account the first use of deuterium-labelled compounds and intravenous dosing to quantify how much cocaethylene is formed in people; the 17% figure is the paper's distinctive contribution and has not been re-measured by this method in any paper read for this card. Its finding that ethanol did not raise cocaine AUC or peak concentration differs from earlier intranasal studies, which the authors attribute to the route (pp. 179–180). Whether cocaethylene adds anything to the effects of cocaine plus alcohol in people remains open: the one direct comparison read here found cocaethylene less potent than cocaine (Hart et al., 2000).

funding.funder: United States Public Health Service grants DA01696, DA12393 and DA00053 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; carried out in part in the university's General Clinical Research Center with support of the Division of Research Resources, National Institutes of Health (grant 5 M01 RR-00079) (p. 181).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors were at the Drug Dependence Research Center, Langley Porter Psychiatric Institute, University of California, San Francisco (p. 169). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A study in which cocaethylene itself is given at concentrations matching those formed from cocaine plus alcohol, in the same people, in randomized and blinded order, with a clinically meaningful outcome (for example cardiac or hepatic measures) rather than ratings alone; and, for the combination, a design with several ethanol doses, both orders of drinking, and a blinded cocaine-alone condition within the same crossover rather than months later.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the crossover conditions)
domains.note: The five conditions are described as a double-blind balanced crossover, but the method of generating the sequence, concealment of allocation and the balancing scheme are not described, and no period or carry-over analysis is reported. The sixth cocaine-alone session was explicitly not randomized and came 1 to 3 months after the others, so for that comparison this domain is high.

The five crossover sessions were double-blind with an olfactory mask for the placebo drink, but the cocaine-alone session was open to participants and staff (p. 180), and that session carries the paper's comparison with cocaine without alcohol. Use of cocaine outside the study is documented on two occasions from pre-dose urine (p. 180).

All 10 completed the blinded sessions, but only 6 returned for the cocaine-alone session and the basis for that selection is not reported; one urinary cocaethylene value in Table 5 is an outlier that was removed, with no sensitivity analysis.

Concentrations and cardiovascular measures are objective and the stable-isotope method is a strength. The subjective outcomes are single unvalidated ratings, intoxication ratings were spoken aloud to staff, and in the one unblinded session participants knew what they had received.

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; many parameters and ratings tested without correction; the cocaine-alone comparison is reported as P values with no means, SDs or figure for the physiological and subjective measures; the abstract, Results and Table 5 give three different numbers for the same fall in urinary benzoylecgonine (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two different questions sit on this card. The conversion and disposition findings rest on a within-person design with labelled compounds and an objective assay, and are the paper's solid contribution; the pharmacodynamic comparison with cocaine alone rests on an open, non-randomized session in 6 people months later. RoB 2 takes the overall judgment from the worst domain, and the unblinded comparator makes that high. Cite this source for the share of an intravenous cocaine dose converted to cocaethylene when a substantial ethanol dose is drunk beforehand (17 ± 6%), for cocaethylene concentrations being far below cocaine concentrations in the same sessions, for the shift of cocaine metabolism away from benzoylecgonine with ethanol present, and for the absence of detectable cocaethylene when cocaine was given without ethanol. Do not cite it for cocaethylene causing any effect, for the combination being more toxic or more harmful than cocaine alone, or for anything about how the combination is used outside a laboratory.

key_findings.finding: With ethanol 1.0 g/kg given an hour before intravenous cocaine, 17 ± 6% (mean ± SD) of the cocaine dose was converted to cocaethylene: a mean of 1.8 mg of cocaethylene-d5 per 10 mg of cocaine-d5 (range 1.0–4.0 mg). The fraction did not differ significantly between the 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg cocaine conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.5 Fractional conversion of cocaine to cocaethylene

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene concentrations stayed far below cocaine concentrations in the same sessions: cocaethylene-d5 Cmax 16.8 (SD 7.64), 30.1 (11.1) and 53.1 (15.0) ng/ml against cocaine-d5 Cmax 250 (73.0), 438 (151) and 891 (271) ng/ml at cocaine 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg. Cocaethylene peaked later (Tmax 1.31–1.55 h) than cocaine (0.28–0.36 h) and had a half-life of about 2.5 h against about 1.8 h for cocaine.
No assayable cocaethylene-d5 was found in the cocaine-only condition, and none in the two conditions without active cocaine; cocaethylene appeared only when both cocaine and ethanol were given.

In the 6 people given cocaine 1.2 mg/kg with and without ethanol, ethanol did not raise cocaine AUC (1030 vs 1010 h ng/ml) or Cmax (968 vs 823 ng/ml), but lengthened cocaine half-life (1.91 vs 1.29 h, P < 0.02) and increased renal clearance (2.53 vs 1.53 l/h, P < 0.02) and the amount of unchanged cocaine excreted in 24 hours (2 630 000 vs 1 490 000 ng, P < 0.02).

With ethanol present, less benzoylecgonine was formed and excreted: peak plasma benzoylecgonine 452 vs 652 ng/ml (P < 0.01), urine concentration over 0–24 h 7770 vs 14 800 ng/ml (P < 0.02) and amount excreted in 24 hours 18 500 000 vs 31 300 000 ng (P < 0.01) in the cocaine-plus-ethanol and cocaine-alone conditions (n = 6).
key_findings.note: The same comparison is given as 48% in the abstract, 52% in the Results and 62% in Table 5; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Ethanol shifted the balance of urinary products after cocaine 1.2 mg/kg: compared with cocaine alone, ecgonine ethyl ester-d0 rose about fifteen-fold (0.324 to 4.71 micromoles), unchanged cocaine-d5 rose to 176% (4.87 to 8.58) and benzoylecgonine-d5 fell to 62% (112 to 69.3), each P < 0.05, while ecgonine methyl ester (58%) and ecgonine ethyl ester-d3 (92%) did not differ significantly.

Heart rate, rate-pressure product and ratings of cocaine and total intoxication rose with the cocaine dose; mean peak total intoxication in the highest-dose condition was 74% of 'the most ever', and peak heart rate was higher in the two highest cocaine conditions than in the lowest.

Ratings of drug liking and good drug effect across time were higher after ethanol with cocaine 1.2 mg/kg than after ethanol alone (P < 0.04), but peak ratings of liking and good drug effect did not differ between ethanol alone and any cocaine condition.

In the 6 people tested both ways, the combination produced a higher time-course rating of total intoxication (P < 0.02) and of drug liking (P < 0.04) and a higher heart rate across time (P < 0.05) than cocaine alone, while peak cocaine and total intoxication, peak heart rate, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure and rate-pressure product did not differ.
key_findings.note: This session was open and non-randomized, held 1 to 3 months after the blinded sessions; no means or figure are shown for these measures.

key_findings.finding: Breath ethanol peaked 55 minutes after the first drink, 5 minutes before the cocaine infusion began, at a mean of at least 0.12 (SD 0.014) g/dl in every experimental condition; ethanol intoxication ratings did not differ between treatments.

Participants' own reported use: typical weekly cocaine about 905 mg (range 94–3500 mg), intravenous by preference for all 10, and on average 13 g of ethanol weekly (range 2–23 g); none had ever sought treatment for cocaine-related problems, and 7 of 10 smoked tobacco, 8 smoked cannabis, 3 used amphetamines, 3 used heroin and 1 used diazepam.

Renal clearance of cocaine fell at the highest cocaine dose (4.58, 4.62 and 2.63 l/h at 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg with ethanol, P < 0.02) and renal clearance of formed cocaethylene likewise (6.43, 5.45 and 2.90 l/h, P < 0.04); the authors say they cannot rule out a temporary cocaine-related reduction of kidney function, since kidney function was not assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: The same fall in benzoylecgonine is given three ways: the abstract says ethanol decreased urine benzoylecgonine by 48%, the Results say the combination decreased the urine concentration by 52%, and Table 5 gives benzoylecgonine as 62% of the cocaine-alone value in moles. Table 4's concentrations (7770 vs 14 800 ng/ml) give a ratio of 52.5%, so the Results' 52% is the remaining share rather than the size of the decrease, and the abstract's 48% is its complement.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader quoting any one figure can misstate the direction or size. The defensible statement is that urinary benzoylecgonine concentration was roughly halved and the amount excreted was about 59% of the cocaine-alone value, with the molar comparison giving 62%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe the plasma benzoylecgonine peak in the combination condition as 'significantly lower (69%)' than with cocaine alone; Table 4 gives 452 vs 652 ng/ml, a ratio of 69.3%, so 69% is again the remaining share and not the size of the reduction.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentage convention is not stated anywhere in the paper and alternates with the abstract's convention, so every percentage in this paper has to be checked against the tables before use.

reporting_issues.issue: No means, standard deviations or figure are given for the physiological and subjective effects of the cocaine-alone condition: Fig. 4 plots only the five conditions with n = 10, and the n = 6 comparison appears in the text as P values alone.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the difference between cocaine with and without ethanol cannot be judged or re-analysed, and no effect size can be computed for the paper's pharmacodynamic claim.

reporting_issues.issue: F statistics, degrees of freedom and confidence intervals are not printed anywhere; the tables carry only P thresholds (NS, P < 0.01, P < 0.02, P < 0.04) and the pairwise ordering of conditions.
reporting_issues.consequence: No result in this paper can be re-checked arithmetically or converted into a standardized effect, and the mechanical anchor check can only verify means and standard deviations.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 reports a significant difference in 24–60 h urinary cocaethylene concentration as 'C,D < E' with no P value, while comparable rows in Tables 1 and 2 also give orderings without P values; and the Table 5 cocaethylene-d3 column is computed with one outlier removed, which is noted in a footnote but not quantified.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some tabled comparisons cannot be given a P value, and the effect of the outlier exclusion on the cocaethylene-d3 recovery cannot be assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: The 7.5 mg cocaethylene-d3 tracer was given in every session, including both placebo conditions, and the authors report that its plasma levels turned out higher than expected or required, with peak cocaethylene-d3 concentrations exceeding those of the cocaethylene-d5 formed from cocaine in all conditions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Every condition, including the ethanol-alone and double-placebo conditions, contained some cocaethylene. The authors judge this unlikely to have obscured differences because the tracer alone produced no visible effects, but a true drug-free condition was never tested.
